# An Inverse Kinetic Approach to Lattice Boltzmann Theory

Despite decades of extensive research and widespread practical application, the lattice Boltzmann (LB) method continues to present fundamental theoretical challenges that remain unresolved. While the method has proven remarkably effective as a computational tool for simulating fluid flows and other complex physical systems, several of its foundational aspects lack a rigorous and complete theoretical justification. This gap between practical success and theoretical understanding motivates continued investigation into the mathematical underpinnings of the theory.

A central unsolved problem concerns the construction of a discrete kinetic theory capable of yielding the fluid equations *exactly*, rather than through asymptotic approximations. In conventional formulations, the connection between the kinetic description and the macroscopic fluid dynamics is established only in an approximate sense, typically by means of asymptotic expansions such as the Chapman–Enskog procedure. The goal of recovering the fluid equations exactly—that is, without recourse to such approximations—defines what may be termed the *LB inverse kinetic theory*. Solving this problem requires reversing the customary direction of analysis: instead of deriving the macroscopic behavior from a prescribed kinetic model, one seeks a kinetic description that is guaranteed by construction to reproduce the desired fluid equations.

This paper develops precisely such an inverse kinetic approach. The strategy exploits the fact that the inverse problem admits an infinite number of solutions, and this freedom can be harnessed to satisfy a range of important theoretical requirements. Rather than viewing the non-uniqueness of the solution as a difficulty, the approach treats it as a resource, allowing the kinetic theory to be tailored so as to fulfill additional physical and mathematical constraints beyond the mere recovery of the fluid equations.

A key strength of the proposed theory is its ability to yield the fluid equations exactly under very general conditions. In particular, the correspondence holds even for arbitrary non-equilibrium distribution functions and remains valid arbitrarily close to the boundary of the fluid domain. This represents a significant advance over earlier formulations: unlike prior entropic LB methods, the present theory imposes no functional constraints on the form of the initial distribution functions. As a result, it offers a more flexible and broadly applicable framework, free from the restrictive assumptions that limit the generality of existing approaches.

Finally, the paper presents concrete realizations of the theory together with a set of asymptotic approximations that recover the fluid equations to any prescribed level of accuracy. These constructions demonstrate how the exact inverse kinetic formulation can be reduced, in a controlled manner, to practically useful schemes. The results are further placed in context through detailed comparisons with the customary LB approaches and with the Chorin artificial compressibility method, highlighting both the theoretical distinctions and the practical implications of the proposed framework.

# A Non-Asymptotic Lattice Boltzmann Inverse Kinetic Theory for the Exact Recovery of Fluid Equations

## Introduction and Problem Statement

The lattice Boltzmann (LB) method has become one of the most widely adopted computational frameworks for the numerical simulation of fluid dynamics. Despite its extensive practical success, a fundamental theoretical question has remained unresolved: how can one construct a lattice Boltzmann inverse kinetic theory that yields the correct fluid equations *exactly*, rather than merely in an asymptotic limit? Conventional LB approaches typically rely on asymptotic expansions—most notably the Chapman-Enskog procedure—in which the recovery of the macroscopic fluid equations is achieved only approximately, subject to smallness assumptions on parameters such as the Knudsen or Mach numbers. This paper addresses precisely this unsolved theoretical problem by developing a non-asymptotic formulation of lattice Boltzmann inverse kinetic theory.

The core difficulty lies in establishing an exact correspondence between the discrete kinetic description and the continuum fluid equations without invoking asymptotic limiting procedures. Traditional treatments impose restrictive functional constraints on the form of the kinetic distribution function, typically requiring it to remain close to a local equilibrium (Maxwellian-type) distribution. These constraints become especially problematic in the presence of strong non-equilibrium conditions and in regions near the boundaries of the computational domain, where standard asymptotic analyses are known to break down.

## The Proposed Approach

In this work, we develop an inverse kinetic theory that is valid for *arbitrary* non-equilibrium distribution functions. A central and distinguishing feature of the approach is that it does not require any functional constraints to be imposed on the initial kinetic distribution. This represents a significant departure from conventional treatments, in which the admissible class of distributions is severely restricted from the outset. By dispensing with such constraints, the theory becomes applicable to genuinely far-from-equilibrium states and, crucially, retains its validity in the neighborhood of domain boundaries—precisely the settings in which asymptotic methods are least reliable.

The construction is *non-asymptotic* in the sense that the fluid equations are recovered exactly, without recourse to a small-parameter expansion. This means that the resulting macroscopic dynamics are not contaminated by uncontrolled higher-order terms, and the correspondence between the kinetic and fluid descriptions can be made rigorous.

## Principal Results

The theory delivers the fluid equations with a *prescribed accuracy*, allowing the level of precision to be controlled systematically within the formulation. This capability has two important consequences.

First, it provides a rigorous framework for obtaining asymptotic accuracy estimates of conventional lattice Boltzmann approaches. Because the present theory establishes an exact benchmark, the errors incurred by standard LB schemes—arising from their inherent asymptotic character—can be quantitatively assessed. This yields a principled understanding of the convergence properties and accuracy limitations of widely used LB algorithms.

Second, the framework enables meaningful and rigorous comparisons with the Chorin artificial compressibility method. The artificial compressibility approach, introduced as a technique for solving the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, shares conceptual similarities with the LB method in the way it treats the pressure-velocity coupling through an auxiliary compressibility. By situating both methods within a common theoretical setting, the present theory clarifies the relationship between them and permits a direct evaluation of their respective asymptotic behaviors and accuracy characteristics.

## Significance

Taken together, these results resolve a long-standing gap in the theoretical foundations of the lattice Boltzmann method. By constructing an inverse kinetic theory that recovers the fluid equations exactly and non-asymptotically, applicable to arbitrary non-equilibrium states and near boundaries without functional constraints, this work establishes a rigorous foundation upon which the accuracy of practical LB schemes can be assessed and compared with alternative computational fluid dynamics methods. The framework thus contributes both to the theoretical understanding of kinetic-to-fluid correspondences and to the practical goal of reliable, high-accuracy fluid simulation.

# Ludwig Boltzmann and the Foundations of Statistical Mechanics

The story of modern physics owes an immense debt to Ludwig Boltzmann, the Austrian physicist whose revolutionary ideas transformed our understanding of thermodynamics and the microscopic world. Working in the late nineteenth century, Boltzmann sought to explain the behavior of gases and the concept of entropy through the statistical motion of countless individual atoms and molecules.

Unlike many of his contemporaries, who viewed atoms as merely convenient mathematical fictions, Boltzmann firmly believed in their physical reality. This conviction placed him at odds with influential thinkers of his era, such as Ernst Mach and Wilhelm Ostwald, who insisted that science should concern itself only with directly observable phenomena. The resulting intellectual battles were often bitter and left Boltzmann feeling isolated and misunderstood.

The heart of Boltzmann's contribution lies in his statistical interpretation of entropy. His famous equation, S = k log W, connects the entropy of a system to the number of possible microscopic arrangements that produce the same observable state. The constant k, now known as the Boltzmann constant, has become one of the fundamental values in all of physics, appearing throughout thermodynamics and quantum theory alike.

Unlike the deterministic laws that governed classical mechanics, Boltzmann's approach embraced probability and randomness as essential features of nature. This shift in thinking laid the groundwork for statistical mechanics and anticipated many developments in twentieth-century physics.

The tragic irony of Boltzmann's life is that he died in 1906, just before experimental evidence—particularly Einstein's work on Brownian motion—confirmed the existence of atoms beyond reasonable doubt. Today, his equation is engraved on his tombstone in Vienna, a fitting tribute to a thinker whose insights continue to illuminate our understanding of the universe.

The construction is based on a Vlasov-type kinetic equation defined on a discrete velocity manifold, endowed with a suitably generalized equilibrium distribution and a collision operator whose functional form is determined self-consistently by the requirement of exact moment closure. We further demonstrate that the theory is consistent with the standard BGK lattice Boltzmann dynamics in the appropriate limit, and that the exact fluid correspondence imposes precise algebraic constraints on the lattice weights, sound speed, and relaxation parameters. # Abstract

**A Discrete Kinetic Theory for Exact Recovery of the Incompressible Fluid Equations: Connections to Chorin's Artificial Compressibility Method**

We present a discrete kinetic framework designed to recover the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations exactly in the appropriate hydrodynamic limit, eliminating the residual compressibility errors that characterize conventional lattice-based and kinetic schemes. Starting from a minimal set of discrete velocities equipped with a suitably constrained equilibrium distribution, we impose exact conservation of mass and momentum while systematically canceling the spurious terms that arise at second order in the Chapman–Enskog expansion. The resulting model admits a well-defined isothermal hydrodynamic closure in which the pressure is coupled to the velocity field through a relaxation mechanism, yielding the divergence-free constraint in the low-Mach, quasi-steady limit without recourse to a Poisson solver.

We establish a rigorous correspondence between this discrete kinetic construction and Chorin's artificial compressibility method, demonstrating that the latter emerges as the macroscopic projection of the kinetic dynamics when the collision relaxation and the artificial sound speed are identified with the pseudo-compressibility parameter. This equivalence clarifies the physical origin of the artificial equation of state, situates the artificial compressibility approach within a broader kinetic-theoretic hierarchy, and exposes the stability constraints shared by both formulations. In contrast to Chorin's purely macroscopic prescription, however, the kinetic formulation provides a locally explicit, algebraically simple update rule that is naturally parallelizable and free of global elliptic inversions.

Through von Neumann stability analysis and benchmark simulations—including Taylor–Green vortex decay, lid-driven cavity flow, and Kolmogorov flow—we verify that the scheme achieves the intended order of accuracy, suppresses compressibility artifacts to machine-controllable tolerances, and reproduces reference solutions with fidelity comparable to established pressure-projection methods. We further discuss the trade-offs between relaxation time, artificial sound speed, and effective viscosity, and outline extensions to thermal flows and complex boundary geometries. These results position the proposed discrete kinetic theory as both a conceptual bridge to classical artificial compressibility techniques and a practical, exactly consistent alternative for incompressible flow computation.
